summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); the first of the ten short treatises (daśa-prakaraṇa); it defines valid knowledge (pramāṇa) as what accords with its object (yathārtha), divides it into knowledge itself (kevala-pramāṇa — of the Lord, of Lakṣmī, of yogins, of others) and the means of knowledge (anupramāṇa — perception, inference, authoritative word), counts perception as sevenfold (the witness plus six senses), subsumes presumption and comparison under inference, holds memory valid, and sets out the faults of argument.
notes: Disambiguated with '-madhva' because other works share the title.

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); a verse work in thirty-two chapters: the first sets out the purport of all scripture (Viṣṇu's supremacy, the five differences, the gradation of souls, bhakti as the means); the second the principles of interpretation, including the threefold meaning of the Mahābhārata; the third creation; and the rest retell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, including Kṛṣṇa's life, in the light of that purport. It closes with the author naming himself the third form of Vāyu, born when 4,300 years of Kali had passed.

title: Sumadhvavijaya

summary: The principal hagiography of Madhva, a mahākāvya in sixteen cantos by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, son of Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya: Vāyu's earlier avatāras as Hanumān and Bhīma; Madhva's birth at Pājaka to Madhyageha Bhaṭṭa; his renunciation under Acyutaprekṣa with the name Pūrṇabodha (Pūrṇaprajña) and his installation as Ānandatīrtha; his tours, debates, journeys to Badarī and meeting with Vyāsa; the conversion of Trivikrama; and his final glorification, the gods hailing him as Hanumān, Bhīma and Madhva and showering him with flowers.

It is the tradition's polemical account; the Advaita tradition rejects it.

title: Nyāyāmṛta

structure.description: 4 paricchedas

summary: Vyāsatīrtha's great polemic against Advaita, in four chapters that follow the four chapters of the Brahmasūtras: (1) the reality of the world — a refutation of the five Advaita definitions of falsity (mithyātva) and of the inferences from perceivability, insentience and limitedness; (2) the Upaniṣads do not teach an impartite, attributeless meaning, and the flawless Brahman is absolutely different from the flawed souls; (3) the means — against the Vivaraṇa view of hearing, reflection and meditation, the Lord is to be won by direct realization born of meditation; (4) liberation is not the mere cessation of ignorance, and the liberated, from Brahmā and Rudra down, are graded. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi answers it point by point.
notes: Four paricchedas, their opening sections and concluding sentences checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.
